utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The late start is due to some technical problems with the transcribing machinery. I hope, Mr. Russo, that it is not the machinery who suffers also from your speed of speech. Mr. Hill, could I remind that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hill.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yesterday, we competed for speed. Today, we will compete for clarity. So, let's move to next day. We were talking, yesterday, about the 5th of August, and we're going to move now to the 6th, and I'd like to refer you to your second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the court officer and the Chamber, Your Honour, all of the references I will be making for the rest of the examination relate only to the second statement, and that is P292.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hill, if you could turn to 0057-7658.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is e-court page 21, at line 8; and the B/C/S translation is page 15, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, in this part of your statement, you describe meeting a SIS officer who appeared at the UN compound gate with a woman. I would like to you describe for the Court what occurred there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At approximately 0600 on that morning, I was at the front gate checking on the intake ever refugees. A Croatian soldier came to the gate with a woman who I believe to be Serbian. She was asking for protection from the UN from the Croats. He wanted me to go downtown with him and her, and he stated he wanted to show that the Croats had not killed all the Serbs. So I asked if he would take us. We went down with him, myself, the woman, and my corporal. We went to her house. We discussed the issue. She could either come into the camp where she would be safe, or I could not provide security for her at her house. After we left with her, the SIS soldier agreed to give us a tour of the town in his vehicle, and I believe the first stop was General Forand's house. He was our sector commander downtown. At that point, on the lawn, I saw two rocket bodies; the first time I had seen them. We checked the house. There some looting. From there, we proceeded, I believe, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'd like to discuss what you found at General Forand's house. You indicated that you found two rocket bodies. I'd like you to describe for the Court, or tell the Court, if you can, whether or not these appear to have been rockets which were fired.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Approximately four inches in diameter, silver, over a metre in length, deployable fins on the rear, four of them. One was bent at an angle. They were both on the grass, and they appeared to be the bodies, not the warhead, of the rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have Exhibit D87.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, looking at the longer projectile in the top picture, can you tell the Court how that compares to the rocket body that you found at General Forand's house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one appears to be wider across, longer, and a different colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now, Mr. Registrar, please pull up Exhibit D83.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, looking at the projectile piece being held by the gentleman in the blue helmet, can you describe for the Court how that compares to the rocket that you found at General Forand's house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same colour. This rocket is wider around in circumference, and the ones I found were not shredded in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, do you know who's in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, Warrant Officer Dellaire, Canadian MP; He worked for me. And on the right is a Czech captain or major pilot, who worked in the Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now going back to your trip through Knin with the SIS officer, can you describe for the Court what you witnessed of the behaviour of the soldiers in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shooting into the air, they were looting across the town. We spent approximately two hours driving around the town. There was various check-points run by the HV, at that point not military police, which we freely got through with the identification of the SIS. The soldier were shooting in the air. At one point, we stopped at a bar. They kicked out front. They had cut a pig in half, were eating the pig, offered us some whiskey. Virtually, every area of town you went to, the soldiers were coming out the of the homes with appliances, TVs, radios, clothes, and putting them into vehicles, that they were steeling from the town of Knin. There was buildings that were burning, there were buildings that were either damaged or destroyed from artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 4911.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When waiting for that, Mr. Russo, I would like to seek one point, some further clarification. You said virtually every where you went, the soldiers were coming out of the homes with appliances. What did you see that happen? Ten times during your trip, 50 times, or was that in a street you would see 20 coming out from different houses and the same picture, the next? I tried to get an image from what you are describing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't concentrated on one area. On any given area of the town you went to, behind the hospital, behind the parliament, below the castle, you would see cars being stolen and soldiers coming out of houses or apartments with material they were loading the cars with. Any part of town you went to, you saw this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you describe it, it sounds as a massive exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, on one area, when we went to a lady's house where he put the sign on, perhaps I only saw three in that area of three or four street, three soldiers. It is more pronounced downtown. There is a bigger concentration of soldiers, but also they were drinking and shooting, as well as looting. When you got outside of downtown, it was purely the looting. They weren't sitting around and drinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And no doubt as to these being HV soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no doubt at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fully uniformed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. With weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, looking at the photograph in the picture, do your recognise -- sorry, looking at that photograph, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's a house that had been hit by artillery in Knin. I took three pictures for my own personal use, what it looked like when artillery hit the ground. So I had a picture of a road. When it hits the top of a house, when it hits the side of a house that. That picture was taken in Knin to give an example of what a house looks like when artillery hits it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have this admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P299, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P299 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now move to page 7661, Mr. Hill, in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, that is page 24, starting at line 23; and the B/C/S translation is at page 17, line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hill, at this particular point in your statement, and I believe you just alluded to it in your explanation to His Honour Judge Orie, you mentioned that the SIS officer placed a sign on a house that you went to. Can you please explain what that was about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some reason, we came in contact with the lady, and I remember she had two puppies. It was at her house. It had two apartments upstairs; a very large, nice house. They had talked. She was concerned about the looting. The SIS man took a piece of paper, wrote something on it, and put is it on the door, right-hand side, which was that apartment. And I asked what he was doing, and he said when they put the signs on the door, the soldiers won't go in. And, as I see in my statement here, there was, right beside, an individual soldier was steeling a car, and the SIS told him to leave the neighbourhood. I later saw those signs throughout the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when you saw those signs, did it appear that those houses were being respected from looting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the ones that I saw with signs, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have aerial photograph 65 ter 5169. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, I'd like you to take the Court through the markings on this aerial photograph, from right to left, if you could describe them by the letter which you have assigned to each?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A" is the area of town where the Serb woman asked us to go to her house. "B" is what I understand as the parliament or the headquarters. When we went by there, they were loading a very large ten-ton truck with documents. And on the right, there was severe burning. Then "C" is part of the supply. There is four buildings that later became the garrison of the HV military police for the town. "D" is the area of the town where General Forand's house was, and "E" behind the hospital is the area of town where the SIS put the sign on the door of that lady in her home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could 65 ter 5169 admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P300, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P300 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, if we could now move to page 7664 in your statement, starting at line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is at page 27 in e-court; and the B/C/S translation appears at page 19, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in this portion of your statement, Mr. Hill, you discuss meeting a military police commander by the name of Ivan Juric. I'd like you to explain to the Court how you met him and who he was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, who was the UN representative to Croatia, was to fly into Knin, I believe, that day. I was tasked to go downtown and liaise with the HV to facilitate that visit. I went down to what I believe was the headquarters to try to find somebody; and, eventually, an individual named Major Ivan Juric -- he walked by us several times actually, but then identified himself as the MP commander. We went into a conference room, I believe, on the second floor there of that building, talked with him. There were several others around the conference room table at the back. There was one individual who, I believe, to be an operations officer, a colonel -- a lieutenant-colonel or above. We did the pleasantries. We exchanged badges, guns, cigarettes. Then we came about a plan to bring Akashi into the air field, the soccer field, that day using HV assets, as well as my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Juric have any issues regarding media coverage of this event?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was one of the sticking points. My commander was asking for press, and Ivan was saying, absolutely, there would be no press.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you indicated, I believe, that he was an officer. Do you know what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing major when I was dealing with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you believe that he had, in fact, more authority than a major, or did you believe that that was his true rank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been his true rank, but he certainly had authority way above that rank in his dealings that I saw with HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Court why it is that you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first case was sitting at the meeting. I'm across the table dealing with him. And the colonel was sitting at the end of the table, and the colonel was saying nothing. He's nodding at the colonel as if he is giving him direction, yet it is the colonel's troops. There is a colonel there, but the major is doing this. That is not how I understand how we work in NATO militaries. It was -- he was clearly in charge, regardless of his rank. Any time I got into trouble when I was caught out in the areas or out in the outside of Knin, any time I used his name, I was let through instantly, whether I was violating a policy or not. If you mention Ivan Juric, we got through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we move on to the 8th of August, I'd like to show you a report which you released, which summarizes the activities of the military police from the 4th to 7th August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter 5168.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And was the report released by you as it indicates.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does that report -- first of all, did you have a chance to review that before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does it accurately reflect the events between the 4th and 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to have 5168 admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P301 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving now to the 8th of August, Mr. Hill, if you could refer to page 7667 at line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is in e-court, page 30; and the B/C/S appears at page 21, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in this portion, Mr. Hill, you discuss a trip you took on the 8th of August along the Knin-Drnis road, and I would like you to explain to the Court what it is that you witnessed there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our camp, there's a road that goes straight into Drnis. We took that road that day because we were denied access to the town of Knin. Along the road, we saw wide-spread looting by civilians, using civilian vehicles and trailers, as well as HV CIVPOL. They were either conducting traffic to get traffic around those that were looting, or they were actually looting themselves. As well, we saw houses that were on fire and damaged all along the route from Knin to Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: When you say "HV CIVPOL," are these civilian police officers, or are these Special Police officers or military police officers? Which one do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall civilian light blue shirt and, I believe, grey pants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court an idea of the scale on which this occurred. Was it impossible for someone to drive down that road and not know what was happening?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I recall, at one point, a CIVPOL bringing a horse out of somebody's barn and putting it onto a trailer of a police car. Lots of plates from the coast of vehicles with trailers that were stopped and were going into homes and filling the trailers. And like I said, on at least two occasions, the civilian police were directing traffic around these ones that are parked, pulling things out of the homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And on this trip down towards Drnis, how far down did you get on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Past the check-point at Drnis, and we were referring to it as Pakovo Selo. If you continue along past Drnis, there's the zone of separation where you have the Serb check-point, Kenyan check-point, Kenyan check-point, HV. We went down as far as the HV one, obviously, they weren't there, and then came back through the two Kenyan check-points and the Serb check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 4902 brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Court what it is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In between the two check-points of the Kenyans down in Pakovo Selo, on the north side of the road, that is one of their team houses for the Kenyans. That is the damage that was incurred [sic] by the HV as they went through on, I believe, the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You said this was damage which was incurred by the HV. Can you explain what you mean about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my error. Caused by the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why you think this was caused by the HV.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had found two Kenyan soldiers that were in this area by themselves. They then described to me that there was another team house south of there that had eight Kenyans in it. They explained they were at this location when the HV came through, and they evacuated from this house to another. When I got to the other house, the section commander, a Kenyan sergeant, was there. He took me around the house and showed me four mortar impacts. When they had come beside the house, he said an HV -- a couple of sections had attacked the house, mortared it. He showed me a brand new military radio approximately this large, 24 inches, with a bullet-hole through it. He said the HV had shot the radio, taken all weapons, and told them not to leave the house or they would be shot. Then he said that the damage at this team house, which I had taken a picture of, was done by HV as they came through on their way to Knin. I later took, at this point, eight of them now in my vehicle, with the three of us, through the check-point at Drnis, and took them back to the because in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could 4902 admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P302 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, staying with the 8th of August, I'd like you to refer to page 7675 at line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is e-court page 38; and the B/C/S translation appears at page 26, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, here, Mr. Hill, you discuss an incident with a United Nations Serbian interpreter which occurred in downtown Knin on that day, and I would like you to explain to the Court what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At approximately 1930, I was advised there was an issue with the UN worker downtown. I took several of my police with me. I went down to the police station, and found a lieutenant HV, who came with me. At a certain point of town, in an open courtyard in between two apartment buildings, there was approximately 30 military individuals standing around. At that point, they were agitated because of our weapons. I had to give up my long arm and my pistol to my second in command, and then I went to talk to who I believe was in charge, who I thought was the commander of 4 Brigade. There was an UN pick-up truck with the right front tire shot out, and it was flat. The back of the truck was filled with personal belongings, and there was an UN employee, a Serbian interpreter, standing there. When I approached the individual, there was an HV civilian police there, Jan, who spoke very good English, and he acted as our interpreter. I asked about the situation. I asked about the situation. The commander showed me a piece of paper that was in, I believe, Croatian, that showed that this individual had served in the ARSK army for, I believe, nine or ten months. Through the interpreter, he said he was a Chetnik and they were going to kill him. All I understood from the commander was the word "Chetnik," and I understood what it meant. Apparently, this individual left our camp, gone to his own accommodation, and was retrieving personal items. We negotiated back and forth that he could not shoot the individual, it was not his responsibility, the individual belonged to me. And, eventually, he agreed that the individual would go with me; however, he said that he could not guarantee the safety of the individual if his soldiers saw him, or my safety which was the first time they said that. He said that any helicopters leaving our camp with Serbs would be shot down, and any Serb men of military age, 19 to 60, who leave our camp would be shot. At this point, we took the individual, we surrounded him, moved him back to our two vehicles, and drove him back to our camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now move to the 9th of August, and refer to page 7689, starting at line 11. In e-court, this is page 52; and in B/C/S, page 35, line 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And at this point in your statement, Mr. Hill, you discuss a trip that you took through the town of Kistanje, and I would like to describe for the Court what you witnessed in that town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the worse town I had seen for damage. There was no inhabitants at all. I believe there was an HV company there on the factory side. The majority of the homes destroyed by either artillery or fire. They had artillery impacts on the outside of the town for the first time, where we saw how they had walked the artillery into the town. There was a massive war memorial, beautiful. It was huge made of it appeared to be granite, that had been virtually destroyed, not by artillery but it appeared as if by sledge hammers. In Canada, we would call it - I can't remember - vandalism, but it was destroyed, completely destroy. It was a massive monument. There was an extremely strong smell of dead bodies, but yet we found none. There was that single company of HV soldiers who were resting by the factory area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you're invited, and you as well, Mr. Hill, to make a pause between question and answer, and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, were there any homes or buildings burning in the town while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You've mentioned a single company of HV soldiers. Approximately how close were they to this destruction, and did it appear that they knew what was going on in the town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the town, there's one area that is some small factories by the main road, and they were sitting to the side of that, all in a line; and, basically, they would have had an entire view of the small town, the smoke, the fire. They were the only inhabitants of that town at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you run into Mr. Ivan Juric on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After we left the town and we were going north, we met him on the road crossing. He asked what I was doing, I asked what he was doing. He then agreed to let me follow him to a couple locations, I don't recall where we went; and then, eventually, we made it back to Kistanje, where we went into a location where there was approximately 12 military police. They were -- had killed a goat and were cooking the goat, and he invited to us eat. At that location is where I saw him have an argument with what I thought or believed was an HV major, who the day before had wanted to stop me from getting in through Drnis with the Kenyans, but I had used Mr. Juric's name. They had a heated discussion; and at the end it, it was clear that Major Juric was imparting on him his direction. The major did not like it, he wouldn't look at me, and then he left. After we finished eating the goat, I went on my way to the Kenyan headquarters, and Ivan went somewhere else in the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Kenyan headquarters that you went to, do you know what town that was near or outside of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Benkovac, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now move to page 7692, starting at the stop of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is in e-court at page 55; and the B/C/S translation appears at page 37, line 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, here, you describe two bodies which you had found near stains on a road, and I'd like you to please explain for the Court what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the hill as you leave Knin, there was a red trailer we had seen for several days. I don't understand or recall how we got to this point. But when we got to the trailer, there was an extremely strong smell of bodies. We looked over -- there is a stone fence. And down the embankment, we found the two bodies. They had both been shot in the head. But what it realise to us is that there was a stain on the pavement. I understand blood-stains from policing before, but it was different there because of the temperature and the type of pavement. But we realised that that was blood. So then we also realised the individuals were shot in head, dragged, and thrown over. But what we realised is that these are stains had seen throughout the sector, beside cars that had been run over with tanks, beside the trailer with all the personal belongings. But we didn't understand what it was or comprehend. At this point, we realised all of those stands that we had seen were blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull of 65 ter 4904.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, is that one of the bodies you found on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could then pull up 4905.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, is that the other body that you found?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could now have 4903.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, is that the blood-stain to which you were just referring?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have 4904, 4905, and 4903 admitted. JUDGE ORIE Yes. Under one number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Whatever the Court likes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, since these pictures are very much related, they will be admitted under one number. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P303, a series of three photos, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, let's move now to the 10th of August, and please refer to page 7698, starting at line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is page 61 in e-court; and the B/C/S translation appears at page 42, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, here, you discuss what you saw in the town of Gracac, and I would like to you tell the Court, please, what you witnessed there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw artillery impacts in the fields leading up to the town. There was no MP, so there was HV. I remember one check-point with HV soldiers by the impacts. The town was fairly well destroyed. Some houses were still burning. There was looting, and there were still some soldiers there. As it says in my statement, they were friendly. Again, large very strong smell of bodies. We drove everywhere with our windows open, so we could identify that. Then we continued to the Czech battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who was doing the looting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: HV soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you see any civilians in this town at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The town was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to page 7699.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's the following page, page 62, in e-court, at line 29; and the B/C/S is at page 42, line 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, this is where you describe an incident at a town, which in the statement appears as "Pecade," but I believe earlier you corrected it to indicate that it was "Pecane." I'd like to you tell the Court what you saw happening there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a town, a small town up to the right, that was burning or was being burnt. There was an awful lot of police there, Special Police and HV civilian police. They had a couple of the Special Police vehicles, large armoured. I believe they're Cadillac Gage 100, four wheels, 30-millimetre cannon; but the cannons were pointed into the town, not out. And we could see people coming out of homes, homes burning, and we could not get near or into that town as we went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The people that you saw coming out of the homes, were these civilians or were these the Special Police or who else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- from what I recall, the Special Police appeared to be on the perimeter, and the civilian police were the ones coming out of the homes, going into the homes, and the homes being on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please pull up 65 ter 4901.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just by way of example, Mr. Hill, can you please explain who the individuals are in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On your immediate left is what HV military police look like; then there is obviously us, the next two; and then the two on the right, that is HV CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when you refer to HV civilian police, are these the uniforms to which you're referring?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Light blue with grey pants.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the individuals you saw in the town of Pecane, were they both individuals wearing these uniforms as well as others?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: These uniforms and, I believe, the dark blue of the Special Police around those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Court an idea of how big a town Pecane is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least 40 to 50 homes, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And would you say that -- or can you give the Court an idea of approximately how much of the town was burning?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say approximately a third to a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have 65 ter 4901 admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P304, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P304 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, let's move now to page 7704 and starting at line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In e-court, that's page 67; and the B/C/S appears at page 46, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, here, Mr. Hill, you indicate that on the way back from this trip, you found a route leading north towards Bihac and Srb, and I would like you to explain to the Court what you believe the significance of that route was and what you saw there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that to be the route of the Serb evacuation. I have been trying to find it as I was travelling around the sector. We were following the tank tracks in the pavement. When we come back down, we noticed there was a large ammunition dump. The landmark for us was a headless horse in the road. There is a large ammunition dump. If you went north by Otric, then we found the evacuation route. It had not been cleaned up. There was a multitude of T-34 tanks, Serb, that were left there. There were several vehicles destroyed, several ammunition trucks that had been destroyed completely. But there was an awful of lot of vehicles that were pointing north that had been run over by tank, and an awful lot of trailers and personal effects strewn along the route all the way up into Bosnia. And we later determined that's what the evacuation route of the Serbs were -- was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you a series of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I would like you to explain them to the Court very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We'll start, Mr. Registrar, if we could, with 65 ter 4906.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, could you tell the Court what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a truck and trailer with SAM-6, the NATO designation for surface to air missiles; so, on the road approximately around Otric, just in the middle of the road, and in perfect condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did that appear to you to be abandoned or was that part of a unit which was moving?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was abandoned and that was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now have 65 ter 4909.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, can you explain to the Court what this represents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: All along the route, it appeared that they were doing a fighting withdrawal. You would come up to a point like this, where there would be crates and crates and crates of ammunition. It appeared they loaded their tanks. They were fighting and would fight back to the next position. And every so often on the road, there was these ammunition piles, which I believe that's ammunition for T-34 tanks which I believe is 80-millimitre. Then you would also find ammunition trucks that had been blown up, or the odd army vehicle that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now have 65 ter 4908.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, can you tell the Court what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an example of a trailer and a pile of personal belongings that was extremely common through the sector, especially on the evacuation route up to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hill, did you see any destroyed houses or burning houses along this particular route?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 4907.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, is that an example of what you saw on that road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would see a group of three or four homes, no soldiers, no civilians around, and the homes would be burning. So I simply took a picture as an example. Another point along the route, once we got to Otric for the first time, we saw all of the fields, all of the animals, cows, pigs, sheep, whatever, had been killed, shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Finally, if we could have 65 ter 4910.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, can you tell the Court what is depicted here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an example of a civilian vehicle that has been run over by either an APC or a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask to have all of these admitted, again, as one exhibit, if there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, this series of photographs will be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P305, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P305 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, did you ever encounter any evidence that there were bodies inside these vehicles which had been crushed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference with some of the vehicles is there would be blood-stains outside of the vehicle, or there weren't; strong smell of a body, or there wouldn't be; and in a couple of vehicles when we looked inside, we actually could find some human hair. It depended on vehicle you were with, but we never actually found one with a body in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to page 7705 and starting at line five.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In e-court, that is page 68. The B/C/S translation appears at page 46, line 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, in your statement at this point, you indicate that you went to a town called Srb, which you indicate was destroyed, and that you saw individuals there looting. I would like you to explain to the Court what you witnessed there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the typical town with some houses destroyed, some burning, HV soldiers coming out of the house. In this case, I saw an individual stealing rakija from one of the houses. They would bring out a couch, for example. The soldiers had virtually nothing for check-points. So, over time, you would see that they would build up their check-point based on what they stole out of houses: A roof, some tarps, or, in this case, a couch. That's basically what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Was it only HV soldiers you saw in this town or were there other individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was just HV soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving now to the next page, page 7706, starting at line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In e-court, this is page 69; and the B/C/S translation appears at page 47, line 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, here, you note that on driving back towards Otric, you saw an orange VW, which I take to mean Volkswagen, flat bed, with bodies inside. I'd like you to explain these vehicles to the Court and what you know about them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we drove north and we found the route, when we passed Otric, we noticed six bodies, four soldiers and two civilians, in a field by a tractor. I wanted to take photos but I didn't, because we had found the route. By the time we had gone up and back gown down, the bodies were gone and we had passed a Volkswagen flat bed, orange, with the bodies on the back. What we later discovered is this is how the HV were getting rid of the bodies. These individuals, I believe, had grey uniforms, and it was the orange, flat bed VWs that were removing the bodies whenever they were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And had you seen these orange VWs elsewhere in this sector?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this point in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Moving now to the 11th of August, I'd like you to refer to page 7709, starting at the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is page 72 in e-court, and the B/C/S translation is at page 49, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hill, in this portion of your statement, you describe going to Donji Lapac, and seeing soldiers whom you believe were from the 4th Brigade. I'd like you to tell the Court what you saw there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just south of Donji Lapac, there is a gas station and there was check-point there. I believe there was four soldiers, 4 Brigade. The town was the same as any other. It was virtually destroyed, nothing had been cleared, and, again, the artillery impact south of the town. Walking into the town itself, you could see that the town was burning, there was flames and smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we move on to the 12th of August, I'd like to take a look at a report which you made, summarizing the events that you have witnessed between the 4th and the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 728.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And was it a report made by you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does it accurately reflect the events you witnessed between the 4th and the 11th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have 728 admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is the date of the document? It shows 4th through 11th, but there is no date of when it was made, that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could move to - just for counsel's benefit - to his second statement. That's at 7640.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Russo. I'm not asking about the statement. I'm asking if there is a date on this document when this document was made, not the statement but the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand that. In the statement, on the first page, it indicates that he provided this to Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk while he was in theatre. So that means it was made sometime during the time he was in Sector South. That is as accurate as I can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's not a date. That's just a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness whether he still remembers. Do you still remember of what date this report was produced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to whether it was close to the last day covered by this report or that there would have been a longer period of time between producing this report and the 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be as close as possible to the final date on the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what do you consider possible in this respect? Are we talking two, three, four days, or are we talking about two weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, I would think, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So shortly after the 11th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's as far as we can go, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will deal with it in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand there are no objections? There was just this question. Then, Mr. Registrar, the report would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P306, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P306 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, moving now to the 12th of August, I'd like you to refer to page 7715, starting at line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in e-court, this is page 78; and the B/C/S is page 53, line 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, at this portion of your statement, you indicate that on the 12th of August, you travelled down to 1 Brigade HQ, which was a Serb brigade. I'd like you to describe for the Court what it is that you saw down there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which line are you on in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It begins at line 19 of 7715.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went south to locate the company position, and that's where 1 Brigade for the Serbs were in Vrlika. There was four T-34 tanks, excellent shape, that had been captured and were being refueled and maintained by the Croats. It appeared that the brigade had simply left. There was no damage. We had found a large storeroom with mines, some had been open. There was a trip-wire across the top, so we simply left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicate that there was no damage there. Can you explain what you mean. Does that mean there was no evidence of a fight or an attack? I'm not sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no damage, there would be nothing burnt, nothing destroyed by artillery. It just appeared as if they'd left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we've covered the events from, I believe, the 8th through the 12th. I'd like to show you a map which you created, indicating some of the places that we've talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 5171.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, do you recall this map?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'll walk you through it briefly, if that's all right. Do the routes, in highlighted colour, do those indicate the routes that you followed, when you were travelling to the towns which are circled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does the route which -- excuse me, does the route which appears in green represent the route that you took on the 8th of August, down to Pakovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does the route which appears in orange represent that route you took on the 9th of August, when you travelled through Kistanje towards Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does the route which appears in blue represent the route you took on the 10th of August, when you went up towards Korenica and also towards Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And does the route which appears in pink represent the route you took on the 11th of August, up towards and past Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the circle which appears at the top of the line in pink with a question mark, where it says "unknown town," can you tell the Court what it is that that references?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went through at Donji Lapac, which is where 4 Brigade soldiers were, they let us through and said, "There are ARSK in the hills, stay on the road." The next town we came to, which I don't know which it is, was destroyed. And from there, we saw the next town north being burnt. I don't know which towns they were. According to the soldiers, past Donji Lapac was Bosnia; but according to the map, it is not in Bosnia. That's why there is a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the distance between Donji Lapac and where you circled the question mark, is this simply an approximation and not meant to indicate the exact location of that town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. All I know is we drove north of that check-point to what we came across as the first town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, the route which appears towards the bottom right-hand corner in yellow, is that the route that you followed on the 12th of August, down to the Kenyan position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have 65 ter 5171 admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P307 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, the final area I want to talk about is on the 13th of August, and I'd like to refer you to page 7719 of your statement. That's at line 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in e-court, this is page 82. B/C/S appearing at page 56, line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hill, at this portion of your statement, you discuss going for a meal with Ivan Juric at the parliament building, and a discussion you had with him there. I'd like to you tell the Court what Mr. Juric told you during that time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had lunch and he pulled up a map. It appeared to be like an officer's mess. And he explained to me on the map how the attack had occurred, with HV and HVO in cooperation, coming up through the Dinara. Then there was a three-pronged attack on Knin. And then across the zone and up north, there was a Special Police brigade, and I believe he said there was a total of six that had attacked. We just discussed how the operation had gone from his end. He gave us some souvenirs, an HV cap badge, Serb money. And at that point, we also talked to an engineer officer, where we identified for him on the map where the 1 Brigade headquarters in Vrlika was, so that they could dispose of the mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And during this discussion, did you ask Mr. Juric the units over which he had command?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had asked what the responsibility of the military police were, specifically on the day that the Croats soldiers had come to the camp. In front of the camp, I saw an individual with a shaved head and a grey uniform, almost like an overall uniform with a black belt. But he was carrying an MP-5, which is a sub-machine gun. It was suppressed with a laser sight. He had an old man at his feet, almost like a dog. I had asked Ivan what he was, and he said he was counter-terrorist unit. And I asked if that was part of the military police, and he said, yes, that they had military police, the HV. But as part of the military police, they had a counter-terrorism unit. I asked Ivan, I said, "Well, who are terrorists?" And he said, "Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Juric make any distinction for you, amongst the answer "Serbs," as to who were terrorists?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He simply said "Serbs." I took that to mean Serbs as the population, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Who will be first to cross-examine the witness? I have looked at your estimates of yesterday. The total is from the minimal estimate to the maximum is three to five hours taken all together. We have available two hours 45 minutes. The parties are urged to be as efficient as possible, and to focus on the most important parts first, and see whether we can finish within this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed. You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay who is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, I'm going to ask some questions now about that man, Mr. Juric, whom you gave us a picture of in your statement, Exhibit P292. And you described him as having great control over the area that you were in, being Sector South. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say authority, not control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Should we just have a look how he got there, because you also make points about how he, as a major, was apparently able to command colonels.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First document I'd like to look at is on the Prosecution 65 ter list, Your Honour. It is 3113.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please get closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Usher, you'd adjust the microphones a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 2nd of August, 1995. It comes from the military police administration, and from its chief, a man called Major-General Laussic. And it's a document that goes to the 72nd Military Police Battalion in Split. Just seeing that reference there, which you can see on the first page, were you aware that that was the particular battalion that Major Juric was commanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All he had ever explained to me was the military police were located down around Split, and then they came up through the advance; not a specific unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 10, which is on page 4 of this document, we can see in the second paragraph that Major-General Laussic, the head of the military police, appointed Major Ivan Juric and a group of officers from the regular military police and military police administration crime section to assist in commanding and organizing the activities of the 72nd and 73rd. And then in the last sentence, something that you had referred to, the commanders of the 72nd Military Police and 73rd Military Police Battalions shall be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric. And you see that there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know if he was commanding as well the 73rd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My perception was, anywhere within my zone of operation, he was in command of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this document now become an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Just checking the document, that's why you have to wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could have spent longer on it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- I was conscious of Your Honours' request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. My problem is a different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original consists of three pages. Apparently, one page is missing, where we have an English version which seems to be complete. Before we decide whether or not to admit it, I would like to get confirmation that the whole of the original is uploaded in the original as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that will be something perhaps the Prosecution and Defence can liaise on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, during the next break. We will already ask Mr. Registrar to assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D267, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It keeps that status for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am interested in how, when you were having these dealings with the military police, it didn't come about that you were aware of what battalion you were dealing with. Is there any further information or anything you would like to say about that, to explain your lack of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I ran into issues or anybody I needed to deal with at all on the military police side, it was strictly Ivan. It never, never came to my attention what unit; and to be honest, it was irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you spend any time with him discussing the structure of the Croatian army military police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, at one point, when we had the visit with Akashi, I spent almost the entire day with him. We talked about, I believe, that he was trained with the American forces. He lived down on the coast. I believe he had two children, was moving to Zagreb. We, obviously, would have talked about structures of NATO, Canadian military, as well Croatian. But to this day, I still do not know what unit he was commanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, and you gave a lot of personal details about him. My question was concerned with whether you had asked him about the structure of the Croatian army military police, so that you were better informed, and I'll add that as a rider to the question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now look at another document, Prosecution 65 ter 3111. This is a document dated the 2nd of August again, coming from Major-General Laussic, who is the chief of the military police administration. It was sent to the 73rd. The subject being the resistance of the 72nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2, I'm taking this from the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see in paragraph 1, Juric is sent with others to the 72nd Battalion forward command post in Sajkovici on the 3rd of August. And, again, that matter, Major Juric is tasked. In the command system, he is superior to the 72nd and 73rd commanders, with regard to the 73rd extending assistance to the 72nd. Again, that confirms what you had believed from your dealings with him. Is that right, Mr. Hill?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That he was superior to the commanders of the 72nd and 73rd?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My perception was he was superior to the commanders, but I cannot tell you specifically which units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Can we just turn to the next page, page 3. He is responsible for the implementation of all military police tasks in the zone of responsibility of the 72nd, and to cooperate and coordinate the implementation of tasks with the workers of the Zadar-Knin police administration. There's further detail there. He is authorised to undertake all measures to ensure efficient and effective implementation of military police tasks in the 72nd and north zones of responsibility. Did you have any conversations with him about his relationship with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any reason why you didn't discuss that with him, when you've given this impression of having long conversations with him and discussing the nature of your work and his work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this document could now be admitted into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, any objection? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D268 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document I want to look at is 65 ter 2224.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 3rd of August, 1995, from, again, the chief, Major-General Laussic, of the military police administration. It's an order on the work of the military police cooperation and joint work of the civilian and military police, and arises from a meeting on the 3rd of August. If we look at page 2, this document which was sent to the commanders of those units, the 72nd and 73rd, whom we've seen Major Juric was commanding, it is an order concerning various tasks. And at paragraph 1, it says about establishing contacts with local police administrations, commanders of the police stations; and paragraph 1.1 concerns check-points. Having introduced the document, it is about that that I'm asking you, Major Hill. In your statements, you describe check-points that were being manned by military police. Did you also go through check-points that were manned by civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go through check-points where they were working jointly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you go through check-points where they may have been on their own without the other, i.e., separate check-points of civilian police on their own?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Separate check-points of military police on their own?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And separate check-points of HV soldiers on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've described the use of Major Juric's name as being total gold in your statement - that was your expression - and that enabled you to get through the check-points. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did that use of his name have the same effect with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I don't recall; but if I was ever -- ever in a jam, no matter what kind of a check-point, his name would get me through, and I can't recall if that was a mixed up with HV police. I don't know. But any time I was in trouble, I got out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And thank you for that answer. The next matter I'm asking you about is your mention in your statement that Mr. Cermak's name didn't have the same effect in the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what context?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, people did not, when you use that name, respond in the same way as when you used Major Juric's name.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't ever recall ever using Cermak's name when I was in a mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that because your experience of using Cermak's name never had the same effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness already indicated that he never used Cermak's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In a bind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not sure what other situation they would be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In a bind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In a bind is a different situation from the normal passage. In a bind is when you are in an emergency or a system of urgency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your objection was about --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where the witness said "I don't ever recall ever using Cermak's name," and then whether that was because of a certain experience of using Cermak name, never had the same effect. I take it that Mr. Russo is saying, if the witness has never used that name, then, of course, asking him about whether it would have a lesser effect when he used that name sounds to be rather hypothetical. That's the objection Mr. Russo puts. Mr. Russo, at the same time, if that is the case, then the witness will certainly answer that question, and that takes even perhaps less time than our dispute about whether the question is appropriate. Did you ever have any experience about how effective the use of the name of Mr. Cermak was? I'm now not referring exclusively to you using that name but to others, or if you ever did it yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never did it. Do you have any knowledge or experience of others using that name? The answer is no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statements, Mr. Hill, you refer to Cermak's authority never being respected on the ground. If I look at page 577731, line 26, in a passage of your statement, where you deal where freedom of movement and restriction of movement, what happened, what General Cermak said, and what happened on the ground a lot of times were as completely different. We've seen your statement, we've all read it, you see; and so we know what's within it, and we know the nature of your statements, where you say, quite clearly, that Cermak's authority and what happened on the ground did not deliver results. That's the nature of your statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. If he wants to point to a particular portion of the statement where he indicates that Cermak's authority was not respected, that's fine. I think what he's actually doing in this question is indicating, based on a statement where he says what Mr. Cermak did and what happened, are two different things. That could be for any number of reasons: One of which is his authority not being respected, another which could possibly be that is he promising one thing and not doing it. I would like a distinction made between those two, or, at a minimum, a citation to where the witness uses the term "authority not being respected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the nature of the statement appears to be clear upon reading. If you would like to seek any clarification or any further details, please ask the witness. But to ask him whether that's the nature of his statement doesn't seem to assist the Chamber greatly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described Colonel Tymchuk tearing his hair out, and having a great difficulty in having what was agreed between the UN and General Cermak delivered to the UN. That's in your statements, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a clarification, every day, at approximately 0900, we have an orders group with all of the senior staff. At those meetings, it is discussed what liaison is occurring between General Cermak and my general. I am privy to what they are discussing and what they believe will occur. That is completely and utterly out of my realm. I am there for information only. So as I am saying in the statement is what I understand they were discussing and was occurring was not what I was seeing when I was out driving around the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never dealt with Cermak. I never had a meeting with him. I didn't write a memo. It was just information passed in the meetings daily about what was supposed or may occur, who they're negotiating with, over what issues, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is what was reported back to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not reported to me. Made information to the senior staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But "report," I don't know in a military context of referring back, but information supplied back to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning further to Major Juric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to finish before the break, but we had some interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which brings you well over the half hour you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I have had some interpretations, Your Honour, and there are ways of doing things. And if we're headed off, it means that we can't deal with them as efficiently as we'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break first, because it is of no use to continue at this very moment. We will have a break and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00, and we will try to start at that time, sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber informs the parties that it has inquired into whether some extra time could be found today or tomorrow, and there are -- at this moment, our efforts are focussing on an additional hearing starting at 4.15 this afternoon, but still we need a lot of confirmations and a lot of logistics to be completed before we can decide to sit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we crossed swords in the first session over a reference that I made, and I'll direct the Court's attention to 577732 of Exhibit P292, and it's line 22, for the benefit of the Court. At line 23: "So that's another example of what General Cermak says doesn't relate actually to what happens on the ground, because all the freedom of movement was controlled by Major Juric, the military police, and the civilian police at all the check-points."
