When I asked the question of the witness, I appreciate in a quick way, because of the time that the Court was concerned with, Mr. Russo interrupted and said there was no example of authority not being respected. Those are the two sentences from this witness's statement, Exhibit P292, where he quite clearly says "because all the freedom of movement was controlled by Major Juric."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hill, I can see you following that. That's what I was putting to you, as what you were doing was using Major Juric's name because you knew that Major Cermak's authority from the freedom of movement passes was not respected on the ground. There it is in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used Major Juric's name strictly because Major Juric's name worked, and that reason only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you knew from the information you were receiving that General Cermak's orders concerning freedom of movement were not being respected by the military police, civilian police, and the military on their own. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And those passages, Your Honour, are within that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us turn to one last matter on Major Juric specifically, because it concerned a passage in your evidence when you said he left Knin round about the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm going to produce here is an exhibit in the case, Exhibit D47. In fact, I will take this shorter, Your Honour. This is an order in the court dated the 14th of August from Major-General Laussic of that date, which the Court has previously seen, which, in fact, revokes Major Juric's appointment down there and he is returned to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your belief about that was correct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I took that in a short way, so as not to waste Court time -- well, not waste it, but take too long. Can I have 65 ter 2224 that I asked the witness to see admitted as an exhibit. I believe I have neglected to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, no objection. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D269 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for the Court's information, D267, which has been marked for identification, the Prosecution have told us that they are looking into it because it is one of their documents that is being uploaded into the system and the Prosecution case manager is aware of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like you to see another exhibit, please, D226, which is a photograph. And while that is coming up, you referred meeting Major Juric in a headquarters. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we have a photograph before us, and you see the taller building. Was that the headquarters where you met him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Had you been in that building when it had been under the RSK forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings within that building with the Croatian army military police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting on that first morning when I met Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any follow-up meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where I was taken for the lunch where he explained the Operation Storm on the map, and I was in that building. When I saw the engineer officer, it was in that building. I believe those were the only times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You referred, after Major Juric left, to having dealings with the new person in command of the military police in the area. Do you remember that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let me just find that for you. Let's put it this way: Did you meet Major Juric's successors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was the HV military police that I was dealing with, not in that building, was strictly the military police of Knin, and that individual was not Major Juric's replacement. He was simply the one in charge of military police in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking at your statement, Exhibit P292, 577685, only for references purposes; no need to be brought up. "I dealt with their liaison officers and also the head of their military police." It's the first line on 577685. "Afterwards I dealt with their liaison officers and also the head of their military police?" Can you explain, first of all, who you were dealing with? Who was their head of military police after Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a major, I don't recall his name, who worked downtown. Later, it was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was separate four buildings over by where the storage was. That's where we would go. That's where we would hand our weapons over. He was not the replacement for Juric; he was just the local HV military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you pointed out on the photograph earlier today where that building was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's the one that you meant. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The liaison officers you referred to here, who were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect their rank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been officers that were dealing with Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk or perhaps Colonel Leslie. They would have been at least lieutenant-colonel rank or above. It would be sparingly dealing with these individuals. I dealt with my own people on my own net or chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And, as you say, it was the Knin military police that you met. Did you meet any other form of military police other than the Knin company?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall, down in Drnis I believe, I was sent to find an armoured bulldozer, which was quite expensive, that the HV had taken from the UN. I found where I thought it was. I dealt with local --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You don't need to give the detail. I'm sorry to cut across you. It is in the statement. It is just the identities or any other information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't ask any more questions about that. That military police, the local Knin military police, did you know anything about their organisation and structure within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any detailed knowledge of the structure of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said in your statement, Exhibit P292, at 577732, line 32: "Obviously, there's Cermak, who I was led to believe commanded all the military assets in Sector South." Where did you get that belief from? What was it based upon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I was hearing in the orders groups with Colonel Tymchuk, Colonel Leslie, and General Forand everyday at 0900.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were at General Forand's meetings where that was discussed. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the meeting was the daily O group at 0900.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Was that the belief then within the UN forces as expressed to you, that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Cermak commanded all the military assets in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by that, do you mean all the forces and --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the military assets of the HV, my understanding, was commanded by Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And do you know where that information came from that was reported to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would have been my understanding from the workings of those orders groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. And on the same page, if we go to line 18, you say: "General Cermak was the head military authority for the Croatian army that we were -- that General Forand was dealing with, so he had the equivalent authority of General Forand. When General Forand said something in the sector, it was done."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Likewise, Cermak. You've seen that statement there. But from -- from passages of your statement, it seems that you have been saying that when Cermak said something should be done, it wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On occasion. And specific examples, as I said in my statement, was the freedom of movement 11, 12, 13, an issue where he said it would be done and it wasn't on the ground. It didn't happen all the time, and I was not privy to what General Cermak instructed on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what position General Cermak held in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know when he was appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between questions and answers, and answers and questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how long he had served in that position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Who is next? Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could just have one moment to get the podium set up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, since we're not certain yet about the time afternoon, you know what my message is, isn't it? Avoid whatever questions which do not assist the Chamber, also avoid ritual dances, closing doors, whatever is in the art of advocacy, and seek efficiency, and that the Chamber receives as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hill.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, I would first just remind us to be somewhat cautious about the interpreters and how quickly we speak respectively. Turning to the period of time prior to Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Kehoe, I will introduce you to the witness. You are counsel for Mr. General Gotovina. So, it is Mr. Kehoe who will cross-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, turning to the period of time prior to Operation Storm, there was a high degree of hostility between the Serb population and the UN, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it -- your vehicles were being taken; and, in fact, a CanBat soldier -- a Kenyan soldier was killed, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your investigation reflected that he was, in fact, killed by the RSK?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three soldiers of the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, talking a bit about some of your testimony by the Prosecution, and I think you have your statement before you, and we talk about P292, and if you turn to page 577644, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Line 18. Now, Mr. Hill, towards the latter part of July of 1995, you note that you could feel the pressure with the soldiers rotating more, "and I guess they were taking losses." You did detect a degree of pressure among these soldiers as they came back into town in late July?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pressure in the sense that we were having a high number of incompetences on the Friday afternoons, when their troops would rotate back. It got to the point where we would close our camp, and nobody was allowed to leave during a troop rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And people were getting nervous, weren't they, the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak to that about my interpreter. On the night of -- the night before the Operation Storm in our bar, a MiG-21 overflew the town several times, and it stressed her extremely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why don't you turn your attention to 77641, line 19 to 21, beginning towards the end of line 19: "This was approaching Operation Storm which at the time we did not know was going to happen. We started to hear, through some of the civilians on the base, people were getting nervous."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you say that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So, at the same time, you realised that there was fighting going on between the HV and the ARSK up on the Dinara, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, likewise, at the same time, you noted lots of -- or more military activity in Knin, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me just go to 577642, and maybe you can help us out here. Line 30. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "We noticed leading up to 4th of August, obviously, we were not aware that there was an offensive coming, but there was more military activity in Knin." So, in addition to people being -- you commenting on pressure and people getting nervous, you noted an increase in military activity prior to Operation Storm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military activity being the troop rotations on the Friday afternoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They increased?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started. When I first got there, they did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So they started in July?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, I'm just asking your assistance here. So, in July, you clearly noticed that there were troop movements coming in and out of Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they on auto more regular basis then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Friday afternoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you also noted in your statement - this is P291, page 3 - that there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, that's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It says, at the end of July, you noted that there were -- or you noticed there was a huge amount of heavy ARSK artillery pieces and tanks and a lot of soldiers in this border area. Was that, likewise, more pronounced as we move up towards the latter part of July in the Krajina and on the border area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And keep in mind that I had made an error originally; and that is Vrlika, not Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about Vrlika. You're talking about Vrlika right down near the Cetina valley. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the equipment, this heavy equipment, heavy artillery pieces and tanks and soldiers that you saw in and around Vrlika, can you explain with a little more specificity, Captain, exactly what you say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we say tanks, it would be T-54s or T-72s, NATO designation; APCs; MP-2s; and the artillery would be towed at 130 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My colleague is telling me to slow down, Judge, and I'm doing my best to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good that your colleagues know part of my responsibilities. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At certain points in time, I take a pause, and I'm just waiting for the interpreters to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back to your answer, you said you saw T-55s, APCs, and MP-2s. What are MP-2s?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is called BMP-2. It's a NATO designation for a Soviet armour personnel carrier, track vehicle, with a 30 millimetre cannon on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about that. You saw those down in the Vrlika area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which is right near the Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, is that a mobile pieces? Obviously, mobile in the sense that it's manned on an APC and can -- as opposed to being dug-in. You put it on the back of a truck, and you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It is a track vehicle with a turret, with a 30-millimetre; a smaller version of a tank, for lack of a better description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the other item that you mentioned was a T-54. T-54 is a tanks, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you, likewise, see troops in that area when you went down to the Vrlika area near the Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would be with the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you saw them, were they moving when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, approximately when was this that you saw these items down in the Vrlika and Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my statement, the 31st of July is when I was down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's move our attention to Strmica. You, likewise, talked about Strmica during the course of your statements. And if we can move to, I guess, your 1996 statement, which is P91 [sic], you note there that: "There were ..." -- I'm talking about the middle of the page here, Captain: "There were dug-in artillery positions in the vicinity of Knin; examples, Strmica, in the hills four or five kilometres west of town." Can you talk to us a little bit about those dug-in positions in Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: North-east, I believe, of Knin, we were coming back one day and we came around behind the waterfalls, which we hadn't done before. And I remember seeing three dug-in ARSK guns in a battery position there that I didn't realise had been there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "dug-in," can you explain to the Chamber exactly what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, the gun is put in a position to fire, so it is not mobile. They dig around it, they can put up sandbags for protection. There is camouflage netting above so you can't see them from above, versus being hooked onto the back of a vehicle and moved quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Captain, that the -- these positions around Strmica had been there for a while?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no way to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you in -- well, just based on your military experience, does it take some period of time to dig into these positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have taken a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, approximately, when did you see these positions in Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but prior to OP Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to 577643 of your P92 [sic] statement. That's the big statement, Captain.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can turn to line 9, and just deal with the paragraph in line 9, which also talks of you being up in Strmica prior to Operation Storm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you say, and if I can read this: "Then there was on a particular day, it was close to the 5th," you meant the 4th, and I think you corrected, "probably the Monday or Tuesday, we got to Strmica because the Croats had shelled Strmica, and there was a Kenyan company position there. So we went to check it out and we actually got up into -- actually went into Bosnia through Strmica almost to Grahovo by accident. We'd actually stumbled into what were the front lines." Now, were the front lines that you stumbled into ARSK front lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They now had tanks, T-80s and T-84s. Just let me stop you there. The T-80 and T-84 are the more modern version of the former JNA tanks, aren't they.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the designation for the JNA tank. But a T-80, for example, is known as a T-72 by NATO Russian, one of the better ones; T-84 is an APC JNA, which is actually a BMP-2, Russian NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to -- if we can orient ourselves a bit, Captain, when we talk about, you know, it's like a T-55, that is generally an older tank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much. Smaller caliber gun, less armour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be pauses between questions and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry. Apologies to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when we're talking about a T-80 and T-84, we're talking about a much more recent vintage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a powerful weapon on them, on the tank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They now had tanks, T-80s and T-84s, I believe, in the Yugoslav version. They had those --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe we left a letter out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They had the BMP-2S? What are BMP-2s?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same as of the T-84.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Same thing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "They actually had them in Strmica. Their soldiers were camouflaged." Strmica, which is north-east about 20 kilometres from Knin, right on the border with Bosnia. "It was obvious this was major immediate staging area. The guys were camouflaged who were going out on patrols. There was a lot of brass on the roads. They were shocked to see us." Now, when you noticed that was a lot of brass on the roads, what did you mean by that, Captain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From their cannons on their APCs, the road was littered with cannon shells. We were actually driving over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, where was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm close to the point -- I'm close to the point where I really have to act as a traffic policeman, just saying stop, proceed. May I urge you just a little break; and if you look at me now and then, I'll give signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know that you said: "From their cannons on their APCs, the road was littered with cannon shells." Now were these shells coming from the ARSK APCs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that this was a staging area, in your opinion. Did you learn what the ARSK was doing or getting ready to do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I saw, they were -- had been firing from that roadway where we first encountered them in the morning. They were sending patrols up into the woods up the hill into Bosnia. We saw soldiers coming back from patrols. Those were the ones that had the camouflage faces, which we had never seen before, and we could hear shooting in the distance up near Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, again, sir, you're referring to ARSK soldiers that you were observing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now one point of clarification. In your 1996 statement, P291, could you go to page 3 of that, sir. In the middle of the page, in the paragraph that starts: "I didn't see ..."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that last sentence, it says: "Other artillery batteries could be seen above the waterfalls north-east of Knin." Now, is that a battery position that was different than the dug-in positions that you had seen around Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's why I asked the point of clarification, Captain. Now, as we move towards Operation Storm, and I want to take you to the morning of the 4th, I take it from your diary that you had been out the night before prior to the actual events of the 4th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out, as in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I guess in your diary, and if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, can we just bring up 1D26-0054.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For clarity sake, this is a typed version of your diary.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see the insert for 3 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I put this up a bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I guess you had been out. What is the Cando, by the way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's call the Can Do. It was a club on the camp that was run by the Canadians. We were precluded from leaving the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, suffice it so say, I guess you had gone out; and in the notes, you had been out late and then you were awoken again at 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when the actual shelling took place, you went down into the bunkers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the shelling commenced at 0500, I went around to the C containers for the Czech. The bunkers were the up hill, and I didn't go to those until later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you went in with the Czechs. And looking at this diary, about six lines down, that is where you had the door open six inches as you watched?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, obviously, it -- you note, following that sentence, that you were a tad nervous, as is understandable.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how long did you spend in that Czech container?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe about 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what you observed, you observed while looking through this six-inch opening in the door?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted in the course of your statement, if I may -- and pardon me. It is at page 577651, line 30. Are you with me, Captain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "They were shooting at us from Strmica." Now, at that particular time, Strmica was under control of the ARSK. Are you just referring to a general area north by north-east?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction with the border with Bosnia, which would be east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you're not intending to say it is directly coming from Serb-held area at that point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted that, I think in your testimony, that you were fired upon by a mortar at about 0630. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly the time; but, yes, it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, can you give us an approximation of just --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 6.30 and 7.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it was later assessed, through an UNMO examination, that that mortar had been fired by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was the job of the UNMOs to do that type of analysis, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, where there is damage caused by shelling or something like that, it is called a battle damage assessment. They would come and assess who actually fired, what the weapon was, so that we could go to the warring faction to say, "Why was this done?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You did that in this instance, and concluded it was the ARSK base that was right next to you, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where; but it was ARSK where it had originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, at that time, sir -- and I would like to ask you a question about 65 ter 436. Mr. Hill, this is a letter of 4 August at 0630 hours, coming from General Mrksic to General Janvier. I welcome you to read the entire letter, Captain. I will not. But the first sentence is: "The Croatian army and the HVO have launched unprovoked aggression against the Republic of Serbian Krajina." Two paragraphs down: "We demand that you take immediate measures to stop the aggression." My question, Captain -- let me take a pause. My question is, Captain: At approximately the same time as the shelling came into the base or the mortar round came into the base, did you ultimately learn that such a letter was being forwarded to the UN by the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I have seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we will offer 65 ter 436 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, I see, from Mr. Russo. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D270 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us -- and let me just go back to your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can put that back on the screen, 1D26-0054. I believe, Your Honour, just for the sake of clarification, if I could just admit this page at this point, if we could just deal with the D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That one page of the diary, no objection, Mr. Russo. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D271 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we move down in this particular document, you note that you did, in fact -- can you see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a larger, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yeah, it is a little tough. Captain, let me know at any point if you want a document enlarged, just please say right away.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just go down a little bit on that, dealing with the 4th of August. You were in the bunker for 90 minutes and then you went to -- excuse me. You were in the Czech container for 90 minutes, and then you went to your bunker. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And at this particular point, with the shelling, you made a decision that you were just going to stay down in this bunker. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- that's where my unit was. That was my bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just reading this document about midway down: "I was sitting on the steps of the bunker, looked left; and by the ISO a big fire blast had knocked me back a couple of steps. The LO," and that was illegible, "caught us. Got a bruise on my lower back. Scared the," whatever, "out of me. Decided to stay in the bunker right at the bottom. Felt weak, lay down, while the shelling continue. At about 7.30, it slowed down." I welcome you to read the rest of the inserts there. Now, while you were in this bunker, sir, you were hearing the shelling, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were hearing it, and we were watching it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you moved down in that, about five more lines to "right before," starting off at "the day," on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It says: "The day was a blur. Shelling is scarey. Start to develop a twitch at bad sounds." In this area, other than your looking out from the door at six inches, do you include anything in there where you are actually watching the shelling from your bunker?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question. When you talked about the day being a blur, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: How long, how fast, trying to do my job, intermixed with the refugees, the shelling, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, given the context of what was transpiring during that period of time, there were many different events taking place during this time-frame; and as you look back, it's difficult to put time sequences and accurate facts together, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, by the nature of my work and my training, it is fairly straightforward to put times to events that occur chronologically, as I've done in my journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in your journal, sir, just looking at the 4th, you don't make any note of actually seeing anything, such as things being hit by artillery or things of that nature, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my journal, if you see midway: "At about 0730, it showed down. We would hear the round whistle in and watch depending on the whistle. If it was close, we would hide down. If it was not, we would stand and watch. I actually have one, possibly two, photos of rounds going into Knin." And then, when you go down further: "Around supper, the shelling was very intermittent. Serbs in the afternoon were putting good counter-battery fire in the hills to the north. While I was watching the town being intermittently shelled in the afternoon with binoculars, I clearly saw their counter-battery fire on the HV guns in the hill that was previously shown on a photograph."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, between the 5.00 a.m., when the shelling started and your -- well, let me withdraw that. You noted during the course of your direct examination that hundreds, hundreds, and hundreds of rounds fell on Knin, between the 5.00 a.m., when shelling began, and the 7.30, when you say it slowed down, how many rounds did you estimate fell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundreds and hundreds and hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give us a ballpark figure, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. Depending on the very first at 5.00, as I said, there was two 30 minute periods where the intensity was quite incredible. There would be lulls. The lull got me up to my other bunker. It would go intermittent, so that we could get up and stand and watch, versus being down in the bunk. But, literally, hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You say it is -- you noted in your report that, at 7.30, it slowed down; and then four lines down: "Shelling continued for most of the morning." When did it begin again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my journal, it appears that it -- it didn't stop. As you see after the O group: "At 1400, shelling continued." My recollection is after the heavy, heavy part that came in the initial attack to mid morning, that it was as we described yesterday, harassment fire, up until later in the evening around the time that we brought the refugees in, when in then picked up again, to the second highest rate of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that heavy shelling went from 0500 to mid morning?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is that where you heard the hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of rounds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very first 90 minutes of the attack, there was years easily hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of rounds at that point and that bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Captain, at that point, by mid morning, I guess we're talking about 10.30 or so, are you approaching shelling that is approaching a thousand rounds coming into Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P151 -- excuse me, P101.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just blow up the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a sitrep, an UNMO sitrep of 4th of August, 1205 hours: "HV shelling on Knin started at on the 4th at 0500 August and continued up to 1040. Total around 350 to 400 artillery MBRL rocket fire were heard by the UNMOs in Knin." Is that number correct, Captain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that number consistent with your estimates when you told us hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of rounds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would believe that's low.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have two minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This also gives me an opportunity to -- well, it gives me an opportunity to inform you about the results of our inquiries. We can have another one hour and a half this afternoon. The OTP took one hour and 45 minutes; Mr. Kay has used 42 minutes; Mr. Kehoe, until now, you have used 45 minutes, net time. Of course, we still have sometime left. I had said, this morning, we have another approximately one hour and a half. Mr. Kehoe, you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you can agree during the next break with other counsel how you'd use your time resulting in how much time you would need, Mr. Russo, for re-examination as matters stand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then at least there's some time left if there are any questions from the Bench. So how to divide the time still avail for this morning and, let us say, 45 minutes to one hour this afternoon, if you could agree on that, the Chamber would like to hear. If you can't agree, of course, the Chamber will have to allocate the time, as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please also try to focus on the questions and try to avoid reputation. I mean, if the witness says "tanks, T-54," and then if your next question is, "Is T-54 a tank," then that really doesn't assist. If you spend a lot of time on a BMP-2, whether it is stuck in a ground, that's really not of great assistance. If, exceptionally, a ferry-boat would be found up on a mountain, then, of course, you should ask bout that. But, usually, we accept ferry-boats to be in the water and to find other things on top of the mountains. That's similar for BMP-2s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, you noted, during the course of your direct, that you had gone up to the helipad to view matters. When you were up there, were you up there with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the helipad. My accommodation and my bunker was just below the helipad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see anybody viewing the shelling Knin from the helipad?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you have seen them had they had been there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I turn our attention to 297 -- P297, excuse me. Captain, this is the photograph that was admitted into evidence in the Prosecution's questioning. This is a ridge where you saw the puffs of smoke, is it not, the circle up on that ridge.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this area, this was the ARSK firing on to an HV position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did this take place on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the course of your work in HQ Sector South, did you learn of other reports, such as from the Kenyan battalion, that they had also reported the ARSK firing on HV positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't learn about what had happened with the other battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, during the course of your direct testimony, you mentioned that you saw air-bursts in the -- on the 4th when the artillery attack was taking place. Captain, are you certain that the HV had the capability to send an artillery piece in there that had air-burst?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HV had artillery. An air-burst is simply the turn of a fuse on an artillery round. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, are you sure that they had that capability?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of what their capability was. At that time, at that location, I saw air-bursts over the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back to the photograph that is on the screen, can you tell us where the ARSK was firing from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you bring up D131; and it is page 5, 1D17-0394.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this was a Defence exhibit that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. Looking at this map, can you identify the fact that you told the Office of the Prosecutor that the shelling that we saw on the screen came from position C1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe that is not correct. I believe the information provided regarding that site was that this was the location of the counter-battery radar, which the witness put in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please literally refer to what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Hill, was shown D131 and asked to locate the area where you saw the counter-battery radar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the supplemental statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the supplemental information sheet that came out of the proofing session. It has not been submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Captain. That was a radar station, but you didn't see the point of where the ARSK was shooting from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us that on the evening of the 4th, a group of Serbs came to the base. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as time progressed -- as time progressed, Captain, moving from the 4th to the 5th, the HV soldiers, after they came into Knin, also brought Serbs to the HV UN Sector South base because those people wanted to come there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs wanted to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's start first things first. After the HV came into Knin on the 5th, did they not bring Serbs to the UN base that wanted to come to the base?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the soldiers and the tanks arrived, I believe, at noon on that day, the 5th, with the HV, they had no refugees with them. My understanding is around later in the afternoon, they started to accumulate at our gate, got larger and larger, until approximately 2300, when there was over 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only individual I can recall coming to the gate with an HV soldier is when the SIS soldier brought a Serb woman from downtown Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to P301. This is your report; and if we can go to page 4, that should be paragraph L.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could blow up paragraph L.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we look at that second sentence, obviously. This is on the 5th of August. It says: "During the day, the HV soldiers delivered numerous refugees to Sector South HQ bringing the total of refugees to about 700." So these soldiers, who informed you that they were going to kill Serbs, were, in fact, on that same day, bringing Serbs to the Sector South headquarters, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand corrected that the HV were bringing them. And the group of soldiers with the tanks, who told me they would kill all the Serbs, do not, to my recollection -- or they did not, at that point, have any refugees with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to 65 ter 4003. If we go to this, this is a report from Peggy Hicks. I believe that is from Human Rights on 6th August, talking about interviews with displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go down to the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: She's talking about these interviews in the bottom paragraph, the last sentence: "These interviews do indicate, however, that at least some Croatian soldiers had been given clear and effective instructions to treat civilians in an appropriate manner." Was that your experience, Captain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we will offer 65 ter 4003 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D227 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Captain, after being up all day, you didn't actually go to sleep until 2.30 on the morning of the 5th, right? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the 5th is the day that you talked about the shelling outside of the Knin base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to D72, first slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you can orient yourself there for one moment, sir. Are you with me there, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that noted that that circled area is the approximate place where that shell hit and those bodies were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were up that road. The shell had hit more closer to the base along that road in front of the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And using that general circle, is that where, after the bodies were bagged, they were put?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were originally put. But if you see the road coming up by the yellow, that goes up a hill beside our camp. Whenever I saw the bodies, the bags were up near the top of that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe, Your Honour, with a marker, he can mark this location, or we can just use this as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can use that. For me, it is unclear in which direction it goes up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please assist the witness. You'll get a pen and you can mark where you -- at least if is on this photograph, you can mark where you saw this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I believe that is where the round hit. This road goes up a hill beside our camp. There is a hill approximately here or where a road goes in. The bodies would be up near that point, as you're looking at the diagram, the left side of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We should tender this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have that marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further markings needed. Mr. Russo, no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D273, aerial photograph marked by the witness, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hill, you noted for us, in the course of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is yesterday's transcript at page 3749, beginning on line 25, Your Honours, going up to the following page, which would be 3750.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes -- and we're talking about these bodies, Captain. They were bagged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, again, you amaze me, that after 3749, the next page is 3750 is totally superfluous. Try to focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were bagged in the black body-bags that we had and put by the side of the road, across from the camp, on a road leading upwards out of Knin." "I was told that HV, when they were martialing to go into Knin for the last night, fired AKs into the bodies after opening the bags, and that urinated and defecated on the bodies. At a later date, the bodies were there for quite some time. I recall seeing them with the bags open, and one body in particular had been -- had feces on the body and the body shot, even though the bodies died or the cause of death was the artillery round." And this line, sir, on 5, "the bodies were there for quite some time." Now, how long were those body there is on the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you note here, "I recall seeing them with the bags opened, and one body in particular had been -- had feces on it," when did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my -- during one of my trips to get out of Knin, when they would stop me go into town, my way out to the frontier was up this road. So, at any time that I would drive up that road over the next several days, the bodies would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, when was the first time that you went out up that road, went out and turned left and went up that road?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to refresh to my notes. I believe it is the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the diagram with the colour coding of the routes? That will tell me exactly when I went up that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the map, if I may, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the one when yellow was to the south --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that is P307, Your Honour. Is that right, Mr. Russo, P307?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue. Meanwhile, we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another, if I could just get this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been on the 8th of August when I was denied access to Knin and then took the road to Drnis and Pakovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the date that you saw them, that you referred to it in the transcript, was 8 August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 168. Sir, this is a transcript of your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then if we can go to the next page and blow up the 6th at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: About halfway through that paragraph, you are discussing the going into town with the SIS officer, and you note: "The damage was not as bad as I thought considering thousands of rounds. Not one body, even the ones from the gate, were gone?" Now, that's what you wrote on the 6th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you wrote that the bodies were gone, and they weren't there on the 8th, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were moved up the hill. When you come out of the camp, you come to a T-intersection and you turn right to go into Knin. You do not see, up the hill, you don't see anything. There's two different directions here, one is going to the road to Drnis and one is directly into the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I believe, during the course of your direct examination, we admitted P291, 292, 293, and 294, your four statements which you said accurately depicted your prior testimony. And in any of those statements that you reviewed prior to your direct examination, do you mention at any point that bodies were on the side of the road and that they had been defecated on and urinated on, at any point in all of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think the Chamber gave as guidance that if something is not in the statement, then it is not in the statement. And if there any question about that, to discuss it with other counsel and then just put to the witness, "We do not find any reference to that in your statement," instead of going first that they were admitted and; second ... Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it anywhere in the diary that you have that these bodies were either defecated upon or urinated upon I'm talking about not the statements; I'm talking about the diary. You can gladly flip the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go another page on that diary to the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will give you the opportunity to review that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can flip the page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Scroll forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go on to the next page, continuing on, on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything in there about the bodies on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these bodies driven over with tanks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't remember seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is a time if you want to take a break, or if you want me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this is a suitable time for you, we can take a break now. We resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with incident on the 5th with these mortar attack, when the bodies were ultimately looked at by the HV personnel, I am reading from exhibit 301, paragraph J: "One rocket launcher, three hand-grenades, and rifles were taken from the individuals." Do you recall that, Captain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the weapons taken off of the dead ARSK from the artillery round?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken into my custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn our attention to the incident at the individual soldiers coming to the gate that you mentioned on the 5th, about midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to, again, the item on the screen and if we can turn back several pages to the 5th, the second paragraph on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, you describe these soldiers as good guys. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted for us yesterday that these individuals, and I'm talking about page 3751, on line 4, in your conversation with the individual that spoke English. "I asked him because he spoke good English what he was doing there." You testified: "He said he had come back to fight against the Serbs and that he had been waiting for this since 1945."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "He was approximately 22 years old." Turning back to your statement in the same paragraph -- or your diary, you note in that paragraph: "They said they had been waiting for this for four years." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now four years is back to 1991 when the ARSK or the RSK, if you will, drove the Croats out of the Krajina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And there's no entry in here about them waiting for this since 1945. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The individual, who was to my left, was one of the two that spoke English who was Canadian, and he was the one that said that he said he had been waiting from 1945. It is not in relation to what this says about the troops waiting since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The diary speaks for itself. Let us move on. You noted, during the course of your testimony yesterday, that later in the day, on the 5th, that you were stopped as you were going into the city - this is 3751, going on to 3752 at the bottom - line 24: "I said we were going downtown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe what seems to be a comment, "the diary speaks for itself," nevertheless triggers for me to seek clarification from the witness. In your statement, you said something about a person who had been waiting since 1945. Now, in your diary, we find "they said they had been waiting for this for four years." Do I understand you well that there was one person talking about since 1945, and that others talking to you said that they, referring to a group rather than to one single person, that they had been waiting for four years for this to happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what now speaks for itself is not clear to me, Mr. Kehoe. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. I will clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand matters to be now that the diary speaks for itself because it is talking about the plural, "they"; whereas, the statement of the witness is referring to one single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my question at the time, and I refer back to my statement of it speaks for itself, there is no reference in the diary about 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, that is always the problem with comments. That we are not as certain about what he is actually aiming at; and perhaps, of course, then that goes without saying that perhaps it should have gone without saying. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time, we will offer 65 ter 168 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Russo? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D274 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I may, Judge, the actual written part of this diary, for which was typed up by the Office of the Prosecutor, is 1D26-0017 to 1D26-0043; and we will, likewise, offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, no objection? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D275 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, going back to the comments or testimony that I was reading, about not being permitted to go into town, this is on your testimony of 3751, at the bottom of the page -- on page -- line 24: "I said we were going into town. We were UN. We were trying to find refugees. He refused. He said it was forbidden. He put tanks across the road, he was angry, and he ordered us back to camp." Captain, approximately what time of day was that? I note on line 18 you said "around supper time." Do you recall the time of day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have exact the page in statement 2, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is actually your testimony, sir, yesterday, from your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "supper time," 1800, 1900, supper time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you know prior to that time there had been ARSK shelling into Knin from Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just cover a few things about this. By the way, during the course of your testimony this morning, you noted that you found some rocket tubes. Do you know who fired those rockets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know when they were fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, basically, the only thing you can tell us is that you found those in and around what was General Forand's accommodation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the front lawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we conclude -- as we conclude the 5th, I turn back to 301, P301, paragraph N, which is page 5 of that document. In paragraph N, I think the page before this, this is on the 5th, at about 2300: "And for the rest of the night, small arms -- SA firing and small arms firing, tank fire, and mortar shells were heard in Knin. It seems that HV and ARSK were still fighting in that area." That is from your report as of the end of the 5th. Now, going into the 6th, the 6th morning was when this SIS officer came with the Serb woman. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the Serb officer invited you come down and ride around with him -- excuse me, SIS officer invited you to come down and ride around with him, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He invited me to go to the Serb lady's house downtown in Knin. I asked after that if I could tour the town, and he obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you went through this town at this time, you observed the town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could turn on this document that's on the screen back to paragraph O, the prior page, in the middle of that paragraph, you note that: "During the patrol, they observed that the damages to the town were not as extensive as anticipated." Do you see that in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, in fact, there was very minimal damage to the town, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more than minimal. Considering the amount of rounds that went into the town and my lack of experience in what a town would like after a shelling like that, I was surprised at how little damage there was in expectation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you went around that town, you concluded that the shelling by the HV had been very accurate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just go to page of your -- P92 [sic] statement, let's go to 577736.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 77 -- last three, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 736, Captain, line 15: "I believe they knew exactly what they were doing and they were extremely accurate." Line 23: "I thought they were extremely accurate." So, while you were going through here, Captain, you concluded that the HV artillery had been extremely accurate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can draw you to line 17 of that page, 36, I said: "I concluded of their accuracy, because of amount of rounds expended on the town, only one hit our wire, and not one hit our camp," which in mind I thought was very accurate shooting for not killing any UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fact of the matter, sir, is that you expected the town to be flattened and you didn't see much damage. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected more damage than I saw; certainly not flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to P291, page 6. It is P291. It's your statement of 23 August 1996, page 6 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just go blow that up first top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Third sentence: "I expected to the town to be flattened; but as a matter of fact, I didn't see much damage."

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that your recent agreement with other counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to attempt to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in fact, sir, as you were going through here -- be that as it may, if I can just go to a subject that you brought on direct and turn to 299.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring that up on the screen -- P299, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this particular photograph is a photograph, I believe, that you stated was a photograph you took of shelling damage in Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GEOFFREY WILLIAM HILL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you put P62 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry for the wait, Captain. I'm just waiting for it to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was just expressing my apologies to the captain while it was coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
